Bedzin Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Będzin, Poland

Not demolished. Będzin's second Jewish cemetery was founded in 1831 after a cholera outbreak overwhelmed the capacity of the town's oldest cemetery; the community purchased the 0.5-hectare plot on Castle Hill for 300 guldens. Będzin's Jewish community, formally organized under a 1583 royal charter from King Stefan Batory, grew to comprise 80% of the city (10,839 people) by the late 19th century after Tsarist settlement restrictions lifted in 1862, still 60% (18,210) by 1921 with representation in the Polish government. In September 1939, Germans burned the synagogue with 200 worshippers trapped inside; a 30,000-person ghetto formed in 1940, with most residents deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau from October that year. This cemetery, in active use until the late 1870s, holds Rabbi Hirsz Rozanis's grave beneath a rebuilt ohel; it was later used for wartime executions and mass-grave burials. A tombstone fragment for Rabbi Jakub Natan - honored for aiding Poland's independence movement, decorated with a Polish eagle emblem - is preserved at the local Zagłębie Museum.
